newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Victorias' woes mirrors Philippine sugar crisis.
newsitem.headline: Victorias' woes mirrors Philippine sugar crisis.

text.p: The financial woes of the Philippines' largest sugar miller was the latest in a series of disasters to hit an industry once mired in complacency and now scrambling to keep pace with changing times.

On Thursday, cash-strapped Victorias Milling Corp secured from its 32 creditors a 90-day moratorium on principal repayments on its 4.423 billion pesos ($168 million) debt. The creditors will meet on Monday to discuss options.
"I think 70 to 80 percent of it (Victoria's cashflow problem) is due to the crisis of the whole industry," Victorias' chairman Bernardo Villegas said.

Domestic raw sugar prices hit a low of 480 pesos three months ago from 800 to 900 pesos per 50-kilogram bag at the start of 1996 due to over-importation at cheaper prices from neighbouring countries, local planters and millers said.
"Victorias, being the largest (miller), was greatly affected by the drop in sugar prices," Villegas said.
The firm, established in 1919, built its fortune on sugar.

Once a top export, sugar funded the lavish lifestyles of "sugar barons" in the 1970s under then president Ferdinand Marcos. It also fuelled a communist rebellion as exploited farm workers were swayed by the Maoist gospel of armed struggle.
The world changed for the barons when Corazon Aquino, after Marcos was ousted in a 1986 popular revolt, launched a land redistribution programme that broke up large sugar plantations.
Of the 100,000 planters now cultivating the country's 370,000 hectares (913,900 acres) of sugar land, 80 to 90 percent of them are farmers owning 10 hectares or less, millers said.
"The days of the sugar barons are gone," said Daniel Lacson, former governor of Negros Occidental, the Philippine sugar bowl.
Victorias was one of the mills that upgraded over the years to keep its leadership. It also diversified into construction, real estate, engineering, shipping and food processing.
Planters and millers say Victorias is now haemorrhaging because its diversification was mostly funded by debt. Victorias denies this, tracing its problems to the state of the industry.
Victorias is expected to rebound in two years if creditors agree to give it a breathing spell, company officials said, adding they expect new board members to help steer the recovery.
Victorias plans to take in a partner that would invest two billion pesos for a 35-to-40 percent stake. Its non-sugar businesses would be spun off, Villegas said.
Like Victorias, other farmers and millers are also looking to Manila to help save the local industry.
They have asked the government to withdraw immediately the 35 percent tariff discount on refined sugar imports from other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Once heavily protected by the state, the industry now reels from foreign competition after years of neglect.
"Cost of locally produced sugar is higher than other exporting countries in southeast Asia in spite of low labour costs because some mills are not mechanised," an analyst said.
Crop yield dropped to 69 piculs per hectare in 1995 from 84 a decade ago due to the lack of new technology. This compares to 120 piculs per hectare in major producer Thailand, officials said.
Millers blamed faltering output starting in 1990 to the land reform programme. They said banks refused to accept farmers' land as loan collaterals due to uncertainties on ownership.
The government has formed a panel to revitalise the industry.
"We are looking at short, medium and long-term solutions to the problem," presidential Executive Secretary Ruben Torres said.

For the short term, state-owned National Food Authority has started to buy sugar at 610 pesos per 50-kilogram on February 25 to prop up prices. Last October, the Sugar Regulatory Administration banned sugar imports up to March this year.
